---
title: "Quiz: fast marching"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. $T$ is the arrival time of a front that starts at the seeds and moves with speed $1/P$; fast marching computes it in Dijkstra's order with the upwind update.

---

**Q1.** With a flat cost, why are 4-neighbour Dijkstra distances diamonds, and not circles?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every path on the 4-neighbour grid is a staircase of horizontal and vertical steps. To reach a point at 45° it needs as many horizontal as vertical steps: the city-block distance $|x| + |y|$, whose level lines are diamonds. A point 100 px away on the diagonal gets about 141.
:::

---

**Q2.** What is the arrival time $T$ when $P = 1$ everywhere and there is one seed?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The Euclidean distance to the seed: the front moves with speed 1 in every direction, so its fronts are circles. With several seeds: the distance to the nearest seed (a distance transform of the seed set).
:::

---

**Q3.** What does fast marching keep from Dijkstra, and what does it change?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It keeps the priority queue and the rule "the smallest tentative value is final", so the order is found on the fly. It changes the **update**: instead of the best single neighbour plus a step, it combines the smaller known neighbour along $x$ and along $y$ and solves for the arrival time of a straight front passing both.
:::

---

**Q4.** Left neighbour $T = 5$, upper neighbour $T = 5$, $P = 1$. What do Dijkstra (4 neighbours) and fast marching give?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$T = \tfrac12\big(a + b + \sqrt{2P^2 - (a - b)^2}\big)$ if $|a - b| < P$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Dijkstra: 6. Fast marching: $\tfrac12(10 + \sqrt2) = 5.707$: a front arriving diagonally needs only $1/\sqrt2$ to cross from the line through the two neighbours to the pixel.
:::

---

**Q5.** The cost is $P = 1 + (|\nabla I|/k)^2$. What happens to the fronts at a strong edge, and what does a larger $k$ do?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
At a strong edge $P$ is large, so the front slows down and its iso-lines bunch up there; regions separated by edges are reached late. A larger $k$ makes $P$ smaller for the same gradient: only very strong edges slow the front, and $T$ approaches the plain distance.
:::

---

**Q6.** How is the minimal path found from $T$, and why is it not restricted to grid steps?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
By gradient descent on $T$ from the target: small steps against $\nabla T$ (interpolated between pixels) lead down to a seed. The steps can go in any direction and the positions are real numbers, so the path is a smooth curve, not a chain of pixel steps.
:::

---

**Q7.** Geodesic active contours (level-set day) and fast marching both deal with a weighted length $\int P\, ds$. What is the difference?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A geodesic active contour moves a curve **downhill** from a starting position and stops in a local minimum. Fast marching computes the arrival time from the seeds everywhere and finds the **global** minimal path between a seed and a target by descending it (up to the discretisation error).
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that $T(x, y) = (x + y)/\sqrt2$ satisfies the upwind update with $P = 1$ exactly.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The left and upper neighbours have $a = b = T - 1/\sqrt2$, so $|a - b| = 0 < 1$ and $(T - a)^2 + (T - b)^2 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 1 = P^2$. The update returns $T = a + 1/\sqrt2$, which is the exact value: plane waves are reproduced exactly.
:::
